- **Two families of per-request, in-memory state only ever grew, and one held secret key material with no destruction path.** Both are fixed without any behavior change to a caller that completes its ceremony promptly.
  - `pkg/keyprovider/frost.FrostBackend.sessions` (build tag `frost`) recorded a `SigningSession` -- including the participant's secret Round-1 nonces -- on every `GenerateNonces` call, but nothing ever read it back: `SignRound` takes its nonces from the caller's own `NoncePackage` by design (see `docs/frost/security.md`; the caller holds and is responsible for zeroizing its nonces between rounds), `ExpiresAt` was never checked, and the only cleanup was `Close`. The map, its `SigningSession` type, and `DefaultSessionTimeout` are removed; `docs/frost/architecture.md` and the package doc no longer describe a server-side session the code never had.
  - `pkg/backend/software.SoftwareBackend.importTokens`, `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric.Backend.wrappingKeys`, and `pkg/backend/azurekv.Backend.importTokens` each cached the ephemeral RSA wrapping keypair a `GetImportParameters` → `WrapKey` → `ImportKey`/`UnwrapKey` ceremony needs, in a plain map keyed by import token. None of the three enforced their own 24-hour `ExpiresAt`, none capped how many ceremonies could be in flight, and only the software backend zeroized on shutdown -- the symmetric backend never cleared its map at all, even on `Close`. A caller (or attacker) that requested import parameters and never finished the ceremony left a live wrapping keypair -- for the symmetric backend, an unsealed `*rsa.PrivateKey` -- resident for up to 24 hours, unboundedly.
  - New shared `pkg/backend/importtoken` package: a generic `Store[T]` that sweeps expired entries on every `Put`, enforces a hard cap (`*LimitExceededError` rather than silently evicting another caller's live ceremony -- unlike a session cache, one entry cannot substitute for another, so evicting the oldest would take a wrapping key away from whoever has been waiting longest with no signal until their later `UnwrapKey` inexplicably failed), and always runs a caller-supplied destroy callback on eviction (sweep, `Take`, `Delete`, or `Close`). `SealedRSAKey` factors out the seal/open/parse/destroy handling the software backend already had for its wrapping keys (private half inside a `*secure.Secret`, opened into a `*secure.Buffer` only for the duration of one `Use` call) so the symmetric backend's previously-unsealed `*rsa.PrivateKey` gets the same protection.
  - A token is now single-use: `UnwrapKey`'s `Take` consumes it -- successful or not, since the wrapping key was already opened to discover a failure -- so a completed or failed ceremony cannot be replayed, and the redundant "delete after successful import" step in each `ImportKey` is gone (`azurekv`'s wrapping key is also held server-side and resolved by an opaque handle as of #1340).
  - Files: `pkg/backend/importtoken/{store,errors,rsakey}.go` (new), `pkg/keyprovider/frost/{backend,rounds,doc}.go`, `pkg/backend/software/software.go`, `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric/backend.go`, `pkg/backend/azurekv/{azurekv,azurekv_importexport}.go`, `docs/frost/architecture.md`.
  - Verified by: new tests in `pkg/backend/importtoken` (token consumption, expiry sweep, cap enforcement, eviction zeroization) and in each of the four backends (single-use tokens, cap enforcement, expiry sweep, `Close` zeroizing pending material); `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost` (and separately under `azurekv`); full `-race` suites green for `pkg/keyprovider/frost`, `pkg/backend/software`, `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric`, `pkg/backend/importtoken`, and `pkg/backend/azurekv`.
  - Fixes #1261.
- **xkey's browser launcher opened any URL scheme it was handed, including `javascript:`, `file:`, and OS-registered handler schemes (`ms-msdt:`, `search-ms:`)** (#1275). `pkg/gui/services/browser_service.go`, `secure_browser_service.go`, and `oidc_service.go`'s default `browserOpen`, plus the `xkey oidc login`/`oidc aws` CLI commands, all passed a URL straight to `xdg-open`/`open`/`rundll32 url.dll,FileProtocolHandler` or a configured browser binary with no scheme check and no guard against a leading `-` being parsed as a flag. The reachable, attacker-influenceable path was OIDC discovery: `pkg/oidc/provider.go`'s `Discover` only checked that `authorization_endpoint` was non-empty, so a compromised or spoofed IdP's discovery document could point it at a dangerous scheme or an insecure host and have it opened in the user's browser.
  - New `pkg/urlsafety` package is the single validator every launch site now runs through: `ValidateLaunchURL` requires the scheme to be `http` or `https`, requires a non-empty host, and rejects a leading `-` and ASCII control characters, returning the parsed, normalized URL to pass to the launcher instead of the raw string. Plain `http` is allowed at this layer — the browser owns the decision to warn about a lack of transport security, and disallowing it would break an operator deliberately opening an internal, unencrypted URL.
  - `pkg/oidc/provider.go`'s `Discover` now requires every endpoint the discovery document supplies (`authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `jwks_uri`, `userinfo_endpoint`, `registration_endpoint`, `revocation_endpoint`, `introspection_endpoint`, `end_session_endpoint`) to be `https`, with an exception for the loopback interface (127.0.0.1, ::1, `localhost`) that development IdPs commonly run on, using the new `urlsafety.IsLoopbackHost`.
  - `BrowserService.OpenURL`, `SecureBrowserService.LaunchBrowserWithOptions`, and `OIDCService`'s default `browserOpen` (wrapping `github.com/pkg/browser.OpenURL`) now validate before launching; the `xkey oidc`/`oidc aws` CLI commands route their `browser.OpenURL` calls through a single new `openLaunchURL` helper that does the same. `SecureBrowserService`'s Chrome and Firefox argv now also place the URL after a `--` end-of-switches separator, a second, browser-native guard against argument injection.
  - Files: `pkg/urlsafety/{urlsafety,errors}.go` (new), `pkg/oidc/{provider,errors}.go`, `pkg/gui/services/{browser_service,browser_errors,secure_browser_service,secure_browser_errors,oidc_service,errors}.go`, `cmd/xkey/cmd/{oidc,oidc_aws}.go`.
  - Verified by `pkg/urlsafety`'s table-driven tests (dangerous schemes, leading `-`, control characters, missing host, loopback detection); `pkg/oidc/provider_test.go`'s new discovery-endpoint-scheme cases; `browser_service_test.go`'s and `secure_browser_service_test.go`'s new cases proving a rejected URL never reaches `execCommand`; `oidc_service_test.go`'s and `oidc_test.go`'s new cases for the wrapped `browserOpen`/`openLaunchURL`. `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_json tpm_simulator ble`.
  - Fixes #1275.
- **`Decrypt`'s RSA fallback ran PKCS#1 v1.5 unconditionally, with no `allow_legacy_key_wrap` gate and no uniform ciphertext-rejected error — the one PKCS#1 v1.5 construction in the service not covered by either protection.** `pkg/xkms/servicer_crypto.go`'s `asymDecrypterOpts` mapped both an unnamed padding and `"pkcs1v15"` straight to `nil` (PKCS#1 v1.5, RFC 8017 section 7.2.2's Bleichenbacher/Marvin decryption-oracle construction) with no policy check, while the identical construction on `Encrypt`'s asymmetric fallback (`servicer_crypto.go`, wrapping under an RSA KEK) and on `WrapKeyByID`/`UnwrapKeyByID` (`servicer_wrapkey.go`'s `resolveWrapMechanism`) already refused it unless the operator set `crypto.allow_legacy_key_wrap`. `Decrypt` is reachable over every transport (gRPC, REST, MCP, QUIC, the unix socket, and the PKCS#11 module's `C_Decrypt` under `CKM_RSA_PKCS`, all of which route through this one RPC) with a caller-designated key and a caller-supplied ciphertext, so the missing gate left the oracle fully exposed by default.
  - `asymDecrypterOpts` now refuses PKCS#1 v1.5 — named explicitly or left unnamed, since an unnamed padding still means PKCS#1 v1.5 — unless `crypto.allow_legacy_key_wrap` is set, via a new shared helper (`legacyRSAPKCS1v15Refusal`) that `Encrypt`'s asymmetric fallback now also calls, so the two halves of the operation cannot drift onto different wording or a different sentinel again. RSA-OAEP is unaffected and requires no configuration change. The unnamed-padding default itself is unchanged (still PKCS#1 v1.5): `Encrypt`'s asymmetric fallback has exactly one construction, so defaulting `Decrypt`'s unnamed padding to OAEP would have made a service-produced ciphertext unreadable by the service's own default decrypt call.
  - A ciphertext that fails decryption once the flag is set — bad padding, a wrong key, or any other cause — now reports one uniform, undifferentiated `ErrDecryptionFailed` (`wrapAsymDecryptError`), discarding whatever diagnostic text the backend's own `crypto.Decrypter` attached, mirroring `ErrUnwrapCiphertextRejected`'s existing discipline for `UnwrapKeyByID`'s identical RSA constructions. Previously the raw backend error text was wrapped verbatim into the response, which is a second, independent oracle channel beyond the accept/reject bit itself (RFC 8017 sections 7.1.2 and 7.2.2 both require withholding which check failed) — confirmed reachable on gRPC, whose `codes.Internal` mapping puts an unclassified error's `.Error()` text on the wire verbatim with no scrubbing (REST and MCP already scrub an internal-status error to a fixed message). A backend capability refusal (a TPM2 raw-decrypt refusal on a sign-only key, for instance) is unaffected and still reports its own text under `ErrOperationNotSupported`, since that names a static capability boundary rather than a property of the ciphertext.
  - The PKCS#11 module's `CKM_RSA_PKCS` `C_Encrypt`/`C_Decrypt` (as opposed to `C_WrapKey`/`C_UnwrapKey`, already gated) is a real, client-legitimate PKCS#11 mechanism reached only through this same `Decrypt`/`Encrypt` RPC pair (`CryptoManager.Decrypt`/`Encrypt` call the transport client, which calls `XKMSService.Decrypt`/`Encrypt` directly), so it is covered by the identical gate with no separate change; `CKM_RSA_PKCS_OAEP` is unaffected.
  - Files: `pkg/xkms/servicer_crypto.go`; tests in `pkg/xkms/servicer_crypto_test.go`, `pkg/xkms/coverage_boost_test.go`, `pkg/api/rest/handlers_transport_audit_test.go`, `pkg/api/grpc/service_coverage_gaps_test.go`, `pkg/api/mcp/handlers_crypto_params_test.go`; docs in `docs/key-management/api.md`, `docs/pkcs11/module/mechanisms.md`, `docs/pkcs11/module/support-matrix.md`.
  - Verified by: new/updated tests covering the default refusal, the flag-enabled round trip, the uniform ciphertext-rejected error (including a regression test that a backend's injected diagnostic text — `"hsm session lost"` — never reaches the caller), OAEP being unaffected, and the unnamed-padding default, on the service layer plus one refusal test each on REST, gRPC and MCP; `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost` for `pkg/xkms/...` and `pkg/api/...`, and under `pkcs11 codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack` for `pkg/pkcs11/...`.
  - Fixes #1283.
- **The PIV, PKCS#11 and FIDO2 auth factors verified signatures against a public key taken from the response, so any key the caller held would pass** (#1282). `Enroll` stored the real key in `enrollment.PublicKey`, but `Challenge` never passed it on, and qrdb's `VerifyFactor` gives a factor only the stored challenge and the client's response. So `Verify` read the key from `response.Metadata`: `public_key_pem` (PIV), `public_key_der` or `public_key_pem` (PKCS#11), `cose_public_key` (FIDO2). An attacker could sign the nonce with their own key, send that key with the signature, and pass. Each factor now works the way the mTLS factor already did. `Challenge` copies the enrolled key into `MethodData`: `enrolled_cert_pem` (PIV, PEM), `enrolled_public_key_der` (PKCS#11, standard base64 PKIX DER), `enrolled_cose_public_key` (FIDO2, standard base64 COSE). `Verify` reads the key only from the challenge. It refuses with `AuthFactorVerificationFailedError` when the key is missing, and it never reads key material from a response.
  - FIDO2 verification now also follows the WebAuthn assertion checks it had skipped. `authenticatorData` must begin with SHA-256 of the enrolled `rp_id`, which the challenge carries from the enrollment, and must have the user-present flag set. It is parsed with go-webauthn's `protocol.AuthenticatorData`. `clientDataJSON` is parsed, not substring-matched, and must have `type` `webauthn.get` and a `challenge` equal to the issued nonce in base64url. The signed data is still `authenticatorData || SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`. User verification is not required, because no enrollment records that requirement. The unused `public_key_hash` enrollment metadata was removed.
  - Wire change: factor responses carry no public key. PIV and PKCS#11 responses are only the signature in `Value`. FIDO2 responses are the signature plus `authenticator_data` and `client_data`. No producer in this repository sent the removed fields; only tests did.
  - Files: `pkg/factor/piv/factor.go`, `pkg/factor/pkcs11/factor.go`, `pkg/factor/fido2/factor.go` and their tests, `docs/auth-factors/{architecture,engineering,api}.md`.
  - Verified by the new `Test*_Verify_RejectsAttackerKeyInResponse` and `Test*_Verify_RejectsChallengeWithoutEnrolledKey`/`Cert` tests in each factor package, plus `TestFIDO2Factor_Verify_RejectsWrongRPIDHash`, `RejectsMissingUserPresence` and `RejectsRegistrationCeremony`. The existing round-trip tests now pass a response that carries no key.
  - Fixes #1282.
- **`xkmsctl frost keygen` in dealer mode wrote every participant's secret share to disk as plaintext hex** (#1337). Each exported package was a JSON file holding `secret_share` in the clear. The files were `0600` in a `0700` directory, but they exist to be carried to other machines, so the share was readable by anything that handled the file along the way. Each package is now encrypted to a recipient key that only its participant holds, and `frost import` decrypts it.
  - **Breaking**: dealer mode now needs `--recipient <participant-id>=<public-key-file>` for every participant, and writes a new file format: `key_id`, `participant_id` and `participant_name` as clear routing labels, plus `package`, a JWE compact serialization of the key package. Each participant first runs the new `xkmsctl frost recipient`. It creates an ECDSA P-256 recipient key in `<key-dir>/frost/secrets`, as encrypted PKCS#8 under the FROST passphrase, and prints the public key (optionally to `--public-key-file`) and its RFC 7638 thumbprint, `recipient_id`, for confirming with the dealer out of band. `frost import` refuses a package from an earlier build (`ErrFrostPackageNotEncrypted`), a package for another participant (`ErrFrostPackageRecipientMismatch`), a modified package (`ErrFrostPackageDecryptFailed`), and a `--key-dir` with no recipient key (`ErrFrostRecipientKeyMissing`). It stores nothing until the package has decrypted. Dealer keygen refuses a missing, duplicate, malformed or non-P-256 recipient, the same key given for two participants (one holder would get two shares), and `--recipient` in participant mode. Every recipient is checked before any share is generated. `ErrFrostPassphraseRejected` now names the local key store rather than the wrapping key, since it also covers the recipient key.
  - The encryption reuses the SDK's existing JWE helper (`pkg/encoding/jwe`): `ECDH-ES+A256KW` to the recipient key, with `A256GCM` content encryption, and the recipient thumbprint as the authenticated `kid`. All of it is FIPS 140-3 approved. Recipient keys were chosen over per-participant passphrases: the private key never leaves the participant, `import` needs no second secret beyond the FROST passphrase it already takes, and no new envelope format was needed. The CLI's store opener is split into `openFrostLocalStore` and `frostLocalStore.shareBackend`, so `import` and `recipient` share one passphrase and one PKCS#8 backend with the share verbs. The SDK re-exports `JWKThumbprintSHA256`.
  - Files: `cmd/xkmsctl/frost.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_export.go` (new), `cmd/xkmsctl/errors.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_export_test.go` (new), `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_store_test.go`, `sdk/go/encoding.go`, `test/integration/frost/cli_integration_test.go`, `test/integration/api/frost_parity_test.go`, `test/integration/api/commands/commands.go`, `docs/frost-threshold-signing/{architecture,engineering,cli,user}.md`.
  - Verified by: new `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_export_test.go` (`-tags frost`). It checks that the recipient key is stable across runs and stored as PBES2-encrypted PKCS#8, and that an exported file contains the share in no encoding (hex, raw or base64) and has no `secret_share` field. A real dealer package round-trips through decryption and `ImportKeyPackage`. Another participant's key, a wrong passphrase, a missing recipient key, a tampered ciphertext and a plaintext package are each refused with their typed error, and so is every `--recipient` input error. The CLI integration workflows now create recipient keys, and assert that the export holds no plaintext share and that one participant cannot import another's package. `go vet` and `go test` are clean for `./cmd/xkmsctl/`, `./pkg/server/...` and `./pkg/keyprovider/frost/...` under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost`.
  - Part of #1337 (item 2).
- **`xkmsctl frost` sealed each secret share under a wrapping key it stored as plaintext PKCS#8 beside the shares** (#1324). The CLI's local store claimed its shares were not kept in the clear (#841), but the Ed25519 key the shares were sealed under came from a software backend built with `AllowPlaintextKeys: true` and attributes that set no password. So it sat unencrypted in `<key-dir>/frost/secrets`, next to the sealed shares in `<key-dir>/frost/public`, and both directories were created `0755`. Anyone who could read the key directory could unseal every share. The wrapping key is now encrypted PKCS#8 (PBES2) under an operator passphrase, and the store's directories are owner-only.
  - **Breaking**: the verbs that seal or unseal a share (`frost keygen` in participant mode, `frost import`, `frost round1`, `frost round2`) now require a FROST passphrase from `--passphrase-stdin`, `--passphrase-file` or `XKMS_FROST_PASSPHRASE`. No flag accepts it as a value. With no passphrase they refuse with `ErrFrostPassphraseRequired`. A wrong passphrase is `ErrFrostPassphraseRejected`, and so is a key directory written by an earlier build, whose wrapping key is plaintext: re-import the key package into a fresh `--key-dir`. `--backend` values other than `software` are refused for `xkmsctl frost` with `ErrFrostWrapBackendUnsupported`. xkmsctl builds no local TPM 2.0 or PKCS#11 key backend, so it cannot hold the wrapping key in hardware; `xkmsd`'s `backends.frost.secret_backend` remains the hardware path. `list`, `info`, `delete`, `aggregate` and `verify` touch only public material and need no passphrase. `info` now reads the public key package instead of unsealing the share.
  - The wrapping key lives in a PKCS#8 backend with `AllowPlaintextKeys` false, so an unencrypted write is refused by the backend as well. Every CLI share verb opens the store through one path (`openFrostShareBackend`), `import` included: it now stores through `FrostBackend.ImportKeyPackage` rather than a second hand-built `KeyStore`. `<key-dir>` (when absent), `<key-dir>/frost`, `frost/public` and `frost/secrets` are created `0700`, and the three FROST directories are re-moded to `0700` if they already exist. The SDK re-exports `ErrPKCS8KeyDecodingFailed` so the CLI can tell a rejected passphrase from other provisioning failures.
  - Files: `cmd/xkmsctl/frost.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_passphrase.go` (new), `cmd/xkmsctl/errors.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_store_test.go` (new), `sdk/go/backends.go`, `test/integration/frost/docker-compose.yml`, `test/integration/api/docker-compose.yml`, `Makefile` (`integration-test-cli-local`), `docs/frost-threshold-signing/{architecture,engineering,cli,user}.md`, `xkey/docs/usage/cli/frost.md`.
  - Verified by: new `cmd/xkmsctl/frost_store_test.go` (`-tags frost`). It covers a passphrase round trip that reopens the store and unseals, and parses the stored wrapping key as a PBES2 `EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo`, not plaintext PKCS#8. It checks that a wrong passphrase and a pre-#1324 plaintext key are both refused, that no passphrase is refused before any directory is created, and that `--backend tpm2` is refused. It also checks `0700` directory modes, including tightening existing `0755` ones, that the public backend cannot unseal, and the passphrase source precedence and error cases. `go vet` and `go test` are clean for `./cmd/xkmsctl/` and `./pkg/keyprovider/frost/...` under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost`.

- **gRPC returned raw internal error text to clients; it is now withheld and logged server-side instead, matching REST's behavior since #1139** (#1258). `errorHandlingUnaryInterceptor`/`errorHandlingStreamInterceptor` (`pkg/api/grpc/server.go`) wrapped every non-`status` error as `status.Errorf(codes.Internal, "internal error: %v", err)`, and individual handlers across the package (`mapBarrierError`, `mapPINError`, `service_ca.go`, `service_user.go`, and others) built their own `status.Errorf(codes.Internal, "...: %v", err)`, so a storage path, a backend library message, or a barrier state reached the client verbatim on any of those RPCs. Both interceptors now route every outgoing error through a new `Server.scrubInternalError`: a `codes.Internal` or `codes.Unknown` status, or a plain non-`status` error, has its message replaced with the fixed text `"internal error"` (its original code is preserved), while the original error is logged at `Error` level with the RPC's full method name via the server's existing `slog.Logger`. A status error carrying a client-facing code (`InvalidArgument`, `NotFound`, `PermissionDenied`, and so on) passes through unchanged. Because the scrub happens centrally in the two interceptors that already sit last in every RPC's chain, no individual handler's `codes.Internal` call site needed to change. MCP already withheld internal error text the same way (`pkg/api/mcp/errors_keyops.go`'s `ErrInternal`/`ClientError`, logged by `InvokeMethod` in `pkg/api/mcp/module_support.go`, go-xkms#1118) and required no change.
  - Files: `pkg/api/grpc/server.go`, `pkg/api/grpc/server_test.go`.
  - Verified by new `TestErrorHandlingUnaryInterceptor`/`TestErrorHandlingStreamInterceptor` subtests: a handler returning a leaked-detail `codes.Internal` or `codes.Unknown` status yields exactly the fixed client message while the original detail and the RPC method name are captured in the logger; a `codes.InvalidArgument` status keeps its own message untouched. `go vet` and `go test` clean under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost` for `pkg/api/grpc`, `pkg/api/mcp`, and `pkg/api/rest`.
  - Fixes #1258.
- **The symmetric and Azure Key Vault backends now bind an import token to the wrapping algorithm it was issued for, and the RSA-OAEP/RSA-AES-KEY-WRAP unwrap logic is shared, not copied** (#1342). `pkg/backend/software.SoftwareBackend.UnwrapKey` already refused key material wrapped under a different algorithm than `GetImportParameters` issued the token for; `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric.Backend` and `pkg/backend/azurekv.Backend` did not check this at all, so a caller could request an RSA-OAEP wrapping key and unwrap RSA-AES-KEY-WRAP ciphertext (or vice versa) against it. All three backends also carried their own copy of the `SealedRSAKey.Use` plus algorithm switch that turns a resolved wrapping key and `WrappedKeyMaterial` into plaintext.
  - `pkg/backend/importtoken` gains `Unwrap(sealed, issued, algorithm, wrapped)`, the one place that switch lives now, and `Entry{Key, Algorithm}`, the store value type that binds a `SealedRSAKey` to the algorithm it was issued for. A mismatch is refused with a typed `*importtoken.AlgorithmMismatchError` (wrapping `backend.ErrInvalidAlgorithm`) before the wrapping key's enclave is ever opened. `Entry.Unwrap` is a convenience method callers use instead of the package-level function.
  - `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric.Backend.wrappingKeys` and `pkg/backend/azurekv.Backend.importTokens` are now `importtoken.Store[*importtoken.Entry]` instead of `importtoken.Store[*importtoken.SealedRSAKey]`, recording the algorithm `GetImportParameters` issued alongside the sealed key. `pkg/backend/software.SoftwareBackend` keeps its own richer per-token struct (it also tracks `keySpec`) but now calls `importtoken.Unwrap` instead of duplicating the switch.
  - A non-RSA enclave -- previously only translated to `backend.ErrInvalidKeyType` by the software backend -- is now translated the same way for all three, since the check lives in the one shared helper.
  - Files: `pkg/backend/importtoken/{unwrap,errors}.go`, `pkg/backend/software/software.go`, `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric/backend.go`, `pkg/backend/azurekv/{azurekv,azurekv_importexport}.go`.
  - Verified by: new `pkg/backend/importtoken/unwrap_test.go` (every wrapping algorithm round-trips through `Unwrap`; a mismatched algorithm is refused with `*AlgorithmMismatchError` before the enclave opens; corrupt ciphertext reports the same wrapped-error shape for every algorithm; a non-RSA enclave reports `backend.ErrInvalidKeyType`); new algorithm-mismatch tests in `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric/import_token_bounds_test.go` and `pkg/backend/azurekv/import_token_handle_test.go`; `go vet` and `go test -race` under `-tags "codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost"` for `pkg/backend/importtoken`, `pkg/backend/software`, `pkg/keyprovider/symmetric`, and under `-tags azurekv` for `pkg/backend/azurekv`.

- **Four server- and frontend-supplied values reached a filesystem path or a generated shell script without validation.** (#1276)
  - `pkg/acme/client/service/challenge.go`'s `WriteHTTP01TokenFile` and `CleanupHTTP01TokenFile` joined the ACME server's HTTP-01 challenge token directly into a webroot path. A malicious or compromised ACME server could have supplied a token carrying `../` segments to write or delete files outside the configured webroot. Both functions now call a new `validateHTTP01Token`, which enforces RFC 8555 Section 8.3's base64url token format (`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`, non-empty, bounded length) before the join, returning the new typed `ErrInvalidHTTP01Token`.
  - `pkg/acme/storage/objstore/tenant_aware_factory.go`'s `(*TenantAwareFactory).ForTenant` built the `acme/tenants/<id>` key prefix from a caller-supplied tenant ID without validation. It now calls `storage.ValidateTenantID`, the same tenant ID validator already used by `pkg/ssh/tenancy`, `pkg/keyprovider/frost`, and `pkg/xkms`, rejecting IDs carrying `..`, `/`, `\`, or `:` with a `qrdbsdk.DAOInvalidConfigError`.
  - `xkey/pkg/gui/services/seal_service.go`'s `blobPath` joined a frontend-supplied blob ID into the sealed-blob storage path. `UnsealData` and `DeleteBlob` — the two exported methods that resolve an ID to a path — now call a new `validateBlobID`, which restricts IDs to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` (matching every ID `SealData` generates, a 32-character hex string, and every hand-assigned legacy ID already exercised by the test suite) and refuses anything else with the new `ErrSealInvalidBlobID`.
  - `xkey/pkg/nativemsg/manifest.go`'s `GenerateLauncherScript` rendered the instance home directory and binary path into a generated `sh` launcher with Go's `fmt` `%q` verb, which escapes for a Go string literal, not a POSIX shell one: `$` and backticks pass through unescaped, so either would have been subject to shell expansion when the launcher ran. It now uses a new `SingleQuote` in `xkey/pkg/shellquote`, moved out of `xkey/pkg/gui/services/secure_browser_extensions.go` (which already had its own copy for the extension-import wrapper script) so both packages share the one implementation.
  - Files: `pkg/acme/client/service/challenge.go`, `pkg/acme/client/service/errors.go`, `pkg/acme/client/service/challenge_test.go`, `pkg/acme/storage/objstore/tenant_aware_factory.go`, `pkg/acme/storage/objstore/tenant_aware_factory_test.go`, `xkey/pkg/gui/services/seal_service.go`, `xkey/pkg/gui/services/seal_service_test.go`, `xkey/pkg/gui/services/secure_browser_extensions.go`, `xkey/pkg/nativemsg/manifest.go`, `xkey/pkg/nativemsg/profile_manifest_test.go`, `xkey/pkg/shellquote/shellquote.go` (new), `xkey/pkg/shellquote/shellquote_test.go` (new).
  - Verified by new tests for each fix, including one that plants a sentinel file outside the target directory and asserts a traversal ID/token never touches it, and one that runs the generated launcher script through `sh` with a path containing `$HOME`, a backtick pair, a single quote, and a space, asserting the literal path reaches the child process unexpanded; `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost` (root) and `codec_json tpm_simulator ble` (xkey).

- **A caller-chosen KDF `key_length` had no upper bound, so a single `DeriveKey` or `DeriveKeyECDH` request could task the server with a multi-gigabyte allocation** (#1259). `types.KDFParams.Derive` checked only that `KeyLength` was positive, and `types.DeriveFromKeyMaterial` — the entry point `DeriveKey`'s raw-input-key-material path and every backend's stored-symmetric-key derivation actually call — checked nothing at all. Neither of the two KDF constructions this reaches bounds a caller-chosen length on its own: the ANSI X9.63 / NIST SP 800-56A concatenation KDFs accept requests up to 2^32 hash blocks and preallocate `reps*hash.Size()` before deriving a single byte, and NIST SP 800-108 accepts requests up to roughly 512 MiB. A request naming `key_length: 100000000000` reached one of those adapters and asked it to preallocate roughly 100 GB.
  - New exported `types.MaxDerivedKeyLength` (1024 bytes, covering the largest key or MAC this service ever derives) is the single ceiling, checked in `types.KDFParams.Derive` (both the bridge-dispatched algorithms and the raw/CKD_NULL pass-through) and `types.DeriveFromKeyMaterial`, so every derivation path — `DeriveKey`'s raw-material and stored-key forms, and every backend's `DeriveKeyECDH` — is capped at the same two choke points regardless of which algorithm or backend it reaches. A new sentinel, `types.ErrKeyLengthTooLarge`, reports the refusal; `KDFParams.Validate` was already checking the same bound for its bridge-dispatched algorithms (against an uninformative bare-`1024` literal) but not for the RAW algorithm, which is fixed too.
  - `pkg/crypto/kdf` itself keeps only the ceiling each construction's own wire format requires (2^32 blocks, ~512 MiB, HKDF's RFC 5869 255×HashLen bound via the standard library) rather than a caller-facing capacity policy of its own; `pkg/types` is documented as the gate anything taking a length from an untrusted request must go through.
  - The service layer (`XKMSService.DeriveKey`, `DeriveKeyECDH`) now refuses an oversized `key_length` as request validation, before any backend or key lookup, so it surfaces as `InvalidArgument`/400/Invalid-params on gRPC, REST and MCP alike, the same way every other malformed KDF field on these two operations already did.
  - The PKCS#11 module's `CKA_VALUE_LEN` (both the generic `C_DeriveKey` template and `CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE`'s template) and every other caller of `DeriveKey`/`DeriveKeyECDH` reach the same gate: they all route through the transport request these two service methods validate, so no separate cap was needed there.
  - Files: `pkg/types/kdf.go`, `pkg/types/types.go`, `pkg/crypto/kdf/doc.go`, `pkg/xkms/servicer_crypto.go`.
  - Verified by: `pkg/types/kdf_maxlength_test.go` (new) — a table of max/max+1/huge `key_length` against every KDF algorithm for `KDFParams.Derive`, `KDFParams.Validate` and `DeriveFromKeyMaterial`, the huge case asserting via `runtime.MemStats` that refusing it allocates no more than a small, fixed budget; `pkg/xkms/servicer_crypto_test.go`'s `TestDeriveKey_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`/`TestDeriveKeyECDH_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`; gRPC's `TestService_DeriveKey_Errors`/`TestDeriveKeyECDH_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`; REST's `TestDeriveKeyECDHHandler_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`; MCP's `TestHandleDeriveKey_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`/`TestHandler_DeriveKeyECDH_KeyLengthExceedsMaximum`. `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost`.
  - Fixes #1259.
- **xkey's FIDO2 touch notifier ran WebAuthn caller data through a shell, giving any web page that could call `navigator.credentials.create()`/`.get()` a path to arbitrary command execution, root command execution when `xkey fido2` ran under `sudo`.** `pkg/notify.CommandNotifier` substituted `%o`/`%r`/`%n`/`%u` (operation, RP ID, RP name, user name) directly into a command string and ran it with `sh -c`; `rp.name` and `user.name` come from any origin's WebAuthn call (`pkg/authenticator/cmd_makecredential.go`) and are replayed unchanged from stored credentials on every subsequent assertion (`cmd_getassertion.go`). Under `sudo`, the built-in `--notify dialog`/`--notify passive` paths (`cmd/xkey/cmd/fido2.go`) built a `su -c '...'` string the same way, so a quote in `user.name` was root command execution.
  - **Breaking**: `CommandNotifier` (`--notify-command`) no longer runs its template through a shell, and no longer substitutes request data into argv at all. `%o`/`%r`/`%n`/`%u` placeholders are retired: `NewCommandNotifier` now refuses a template containing any of them with a new typed error, `ErrTemplatePlaceholder`, so an old config fails loudly at startup instead of silently changing behaviour. The template is still split into argv once, at construction (`pkg/notify.splitCommandTemplate`, shell-like whitespace/quote rules), and that argv runs exactly as given, unmodified, via `exec.Command` — never through a shell. Request data reaches the command through exactly one channel: the `XKEY_OPERATION`/`XKEY_RP_ID`/`XKEY_RP_NAME`/`XKEY_USER_NAME` environment variables, for example `sh -c 'notify-send "Touch required" "$XKEY_RP_ID"'` — a shell expands a double-quoted variable without re-parsing its value as code.
  - An earlier version of this fix kept `%o`/`%r`/`%n`/`%u` argv substitution and tried to protect only a shell's `-c` script argument by name-matching known interpreters (`sh`, `bash`, ...). Review found that denylist incomplete and unfixable by extension: clustered shell flags (`sh -ec`), wrapper commands (`env`, `nice`, `nohup`, `sudo`, `doas`, `runuser -- `), other language interpreters (`python3 -c`, `perl -e`, `node -e`, `pwsh -Command`), and flag injection into a command with no interpreter at all (`notify-send` given a `UserName` of `--app-name=x`) all bypass a name-based denylist. Removing argv substitution entirely, rather than trying to enumerate every way to reach it, closes the whole class.
  - The `--notify dialog`/`--notify passive` sudo paths no longer build a `su -c` string at all. `cmd/xkey/cmd/fido2_sudo_notify.go` adds `sudoDialogNotifier`/`sudoPassiveNotifier`, which run `runuser -u <user> -- env ... zenity ...`/`notify-send ...` directly, with every caller-controlled value in its own fixed argv element (`--text=<value>`); the dialog's approve-then-touch sequencing (previously a shell `&&`) is ordinary Go control flow: run zenity, check its exit status, then run `xkey touch --socket ...` only on approval. `--no-markup` on zenity stops Pango markup injection, and `--` before notify-send's summary/body stops a value starting with `-` from being parsed as a flag.
  - An invalid `notify_command` (placeholders, empty, unterminated quote) now stops `xkey fido2` at startup with `ErrFIDO2InvalidNotifyCommand`. Previously `createNotifier` logged a warning and ran with no touch notifications at all.
  - Caller-controlled display fields (operation, RP ID, RP name, user name) are additionally run through `notify.SanitizeTouchRequest`, which strips control characters and bounds each field to 256 runes before it reaches any notifier or the environment — presentation hygiene, not the injection fix itself.
  - Files: `pkg/notify/command.go`, `pkg/notify/sanitize.go` (new), `pkg/notify/errors.go`, `pkg/notify/notifier.go`, `cmd/xkey/cmd/fido2.go`, `cmd/xkey/cmd/fido2_sudo_notify.go` (new), plus documentation: `docs/fido2/README.md`, `docs/password/cli.md`, `docs/virtual-authenticator/cli.md`, `skills/xkey-agent/reference/cli.md` (regenerated via `make skill-reference`).
  - Verified by `pkg/notify/command_test.go` and `cmd/xkey/cmd/fido2_sudo_notify_test.go`: a template containing `%o`/`%r`/`%n`/`%u` is refused; argv is exactly the operator's split template, unmodified, regardless of request content; hostile `rp.name`/`user.name` values (`'`, `"`, `;`, `$(id)`, backticks, a leading `-`, `--help`) reach the command only via environment variables, verbatim; template splitting and its quoting/escaping rules; and the sudo dialog's approve-runs-touch / deny-skips-touch sequencing and hostile-value argv construction via a fake `runuser` on `PATH`. `go vet` and `gofmt` clean under `codec_json tpm_simulator ble`.
  - Fixes #1273.
- **Three phone-pairing weaknesses let a corrupt record, a second BLE central, or a peer-chosen name undermine the pinned-key guarantee `xkey device pair` is supposed to give** (#1307).
  - `phone.NewBLEPeripheral` accepted an `ExpectedRemoteStatic` that decoded to nothing usable: `device_listen.go` base64-decodes the paired device's stored `NoisePublicKey`, and decoding `""` yields a non-nil, zero-length slice rather than an error, which the Noise session's `PeerStaticKey` then silently treats as "nothing to pin" — a corrupt or empty stored key downgraded a supposedly pinned connection to an unpinned one. `NewBLEPeripheral` now refuses a supplied `ExpectedRemoteStatic` that is not empty-and-nil (unpinned, still allowed) or exactly `pairing.NoiseKeySize` bytes, returning `ErrPeripheralInvalidPin`; `device listen` performs the same check on the decoded key before any TPM/bridge setup runs, returning `ErrDevicePinInvalid`.
  - `BLEPeripheral`'s GATT control-point `WriteEvent` fed every write into one shared `incomingData` channel and reassembler regardless of which central sent it, so a second central connected during a session could inject fragments into the legitimate phone's handshake or request stream. `handleWrite` now binds the session to whichever central's write arrives first and drops a write reporting a different one (logged at debug); the binding is reset when a session starts and again when it ends, so the next session is not refused for the previous one's central. This corrects the write path everywhere `bluetooth.Connection` identifies the writer per-connection (the `hci`/`ninafw`/`cyw43439` backends); BlueZ's D-Bus backend (`gatts_linux.go`, what a normal Linux build compiles) does not expose per-write connection identity at all and reports every write as the same handle, which is a documented upstream limitation this change cannot itself close.
  - The paired-device record's `Name` is peer-chosen and untrusted — the CLI stores the BLE-advertised local name, the GUI stores the name the phone returns in the pairing confirmation RPC — yet both use it as the record's lookup key. An empty, oversized, or control-character name could reach storage and a display prompt unvalidated; two devices given the same name made every later name lookup silently take the first match, deciding (by list order, which an attacker choosing when to pair controls) which pinned key a connection trusted; and the CLI's `--force` re-pair deleted *every* record sharing the advertised name, including an unrelated device's own pairing. `pkg/pairing` gained `ValidateDeviceName` (length bound, printable, no control characters), `ConflictingPairedDevice` (refuses a name already used by a different device — matched by neither address nor pinned key), `SamePairedDeviceIndices` / `ReplacePairedDevices` (identify and collapse every stale record for the *same* device, matched by address or pinned key so Android's RPA address rotation and a reinstall's key rotation both resolve correctly), and `FindPairedDeviceByName` (refuses an ambiguous name instead of returning the first match). The CLI's `device pair` and `device listen`, and the GUI's `Pair`/`Connect`/`Unpair`, all now go through these instead of ad hoc name comparisons; no storage migration was needed — the paired-device slice shape is unchanged, only how it is searched and mutated.
  - Files: `xkey/pkg/phone/ble_peripheral.go`, `xkey/cmd/xkey/cmd/device_listen.go`, `xkey/cmd/xkey/cmd/device_pair.go`, `xkey/pkg/gui/services/phone_service.go`, `xkey/pkg/pairing/device_naming.go` (new).
  - Verified by `TestNewBLEPeripheral_RejectsInvalidPin`, `TestBLEPeripheral_HandleWrite_BindsToFirstCentral`, `TestBLEPeripheral_ResetCentralBinding_AllowsNextCentral`, `TestRunDeviceListen_RefusesEmptyPinnedKey`, `TestRunDeviceListen_RefusesWrongLengthPinnedKey`, `TestRunDeviceListen_RefusesAmbiguousDeviceName`, `TestResolvePairedDevices_RefusesNameCollisionWithDifferentKey`, `TestResolvePairedDevices_ReplacesByKeyAcrossAddressRotation`, `TestResolvePairedDevices_ForceNeverDeletesAnUnrelatedSameNamedDevice`, `TestPairRefusesInvalidDeviceName`, `TestPairRefusesNameCollisionWithDifferentDevice`, `TestPairReplacesStaleRecordAcrossAddressRotation`, `TestPhoneService_Unpair_AmbiguousNameRefuses`, `TestPhoneService_Connect_AmbiguousNameRefuses`, and the `pkg/pairing` `device_naming_test.go` suite; `go vet -tags "codec_json tpm_simulator ble" ./pkg/phone/... ./pkg/gui/services/... ./cmd/xkey/cmd/...` and `gofmt` clean.
- **The PKCS#11 auth factor recorded a signing mechanism at enrollment but never checked it at verification** (#1289 item 4). `Enroll` stored `mechanism` in the enrollment's metadata and `Challenge` already copied it into `MethodData["mechanism"]`, but `Verify` never read it: it chose ECDSA vs. RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 purely from the enrolled key's Go type, so a corrupted or hand-edited challenge whose mechanism no longer matched the enrolled key's algorithm, or a response that named a different mechanism than the one recorded at enrollment, verified anyway as long as the signature itself checked out. `Verify` now reads the mechanism from `challenge.MethodData["mechanism"]` — never from the response — and refuses with `AuthFactorVerificationFailedError` when it is missing, when its family (`CKM_ECDSA*` vs. an `RSA` mechanism) is inconsistent with the enrolled key's algorithm, or when `response.Metadata["mechanism"]` names a different mechanism than the enrolled one. It never selects *how* a signature is checked from anything the response supplies; the mechanism only ever gates a refusal.
  - `Enroll` now applies the same family check to the mechanism it is about to record, refusing an EC key enrolled with an RSA mechanism or an RSA key enrolled with an ECDSA mechanism. This also fixed a latent bug: `Config.DefaultMechanism` (`CKM_ECDSA_SHA256`) was applied to every enrollment regardless of key type, so an RSA key enrolled without an explicit `"mechanism"` MethodParam was recorded with an ECDSA mechanism. RSA enrollments without an explicit mechanism now default to `CKM_SHA256_RSA_PKCS`.
  - Files: `pkg/factor/pkcs11/factor.go` and its tests, `pkg/factor/registry_wiring_test.go` (one existing test used a semantically-inconsistent mechanism/key-type pair purely to prove config plumbing; switched to a same-family mechanism), `docs/auth-factors/{architecture,engineering}.md`.
  - Verified by `TestEnroll_RejectsMechanismInconsistentWithKeyType`, `TestEnroll_RSADefaultsToAnRSAMechanism`, `TestVerify_RejectsResponseNamingADifferentMechanism`, `TestVerify_AcceptsResponseNamingTheEnrolledMechanism`, `TestVerify_RejectsChallengeWithoutMechanism`, `TestVerify_RejectsChallengeWithInconsistentMechanism` and `TestMechanismFamily` in `pkg/factor/pkcs11`.
  - Fixes #1289 (item 4).
- **Encrypted PKCS#8 key storage now derives its wrapping key with 600,000 PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 iterations, not 10,000.** `pkg/encoding/pkcs8.go` and `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8/pkcs8.go` each pinned their own `*pkcs8.Opts` with `IterationCount: 10000` — a duplicate that could (and, absent this fix, eventually would) drift out of step, silently giving one caller a weaker iteration count than the other. 10,000 was already below OWASP's 2023 recommendation for PBKDF2-SHA256; a stolen encrypted key blob was cheaper to brute-force than it should be. There is now a single shared value, `encoding.PKCS8EncryptOpts` (`pkg/encoding/pkcs8.go`), at 600,000 iterations — OWASP's 2023 figure, well above `pkg/crypto/kdf.MinPBKDF2Iterations`, enforced by a compile-time assertion — which `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8` now imports instead of keeping its own copy. No migration is needed: PBES2 records its own iteration count in the encrypted blob, so a key encrypted at 10,000 iterations by an earlier release stays decryptable exactly as before; only newly encrypted keys use the higher count.
  - Files: `pkg/encoding/pkcs8.go`, `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8/pkcs8.go`.
  - Verified by `pkg/encoding/pkcs8_test.go`'s new `TestEncodePKCS8_IterationCount` (parses the PBES2 parameters out of a freshly encrypted blob and asserts the iteration count is the new shared constant) and `TestDecodePKCS8_LegacyIterationCount` (encrypts a blob at the old 10,000-iteration `*pkcs8.Opts` directly, then confirms `DecodePKCS8` still decrypts it). Raising the iteration count 60x has a measured cost: `pkg/encoding`'s suite went from an estimated ~5.6s to 8.3s (five encrypt/decrypt round trips at ~0.55s each instead of ~0.01s); `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8`'s 21.8s suite is unaffected within measurement noise, since only one of its tests encrypts a key. Both stay well under the 2x/10s regression bar; no test-only iteration-count override was added.
  - Fixes #1286.
- **Refresh-token rotation never re-checked the user, and disabling or deleting an account did not end its already-issued sessions** (#1297). `pkg/auth/token.Issuer.Refresh` rebuilt the identity solely from the refresh token's own claims (`identityFromClaims`) and minted a new access token from that snapshot; a user disabled or deleted after login kept refreshing indefinitely, on the stale roles it logged in with, until the refresh token's own long TTL expired. `handleAuthRefresh` (`pkg/api/rest/handlers_auth.go`) did no user lookup of its own, so this was the only enforcement point on the wire. `Issuer.Refresh` now re-checks the token's subject through an optional `token.UserResolver` before any rotation is attempted: refusal (account not `qrdbsdk.LifecycleActive`, deleted, or unresolvable) is `*UserRecheckFailedError`, mapped by the REST handler to the same generic 401 as every other refresh refusal, so a presented token never reveals *why* it was refused. On success the rotated access token carries the account's CURRENT roles, not the login-time snapshot — a role change now reaches the very next refresh. `pkg/auth.QRDBUserResolver` is the production resolver, resolving the qrdb-backed identity plane the same way `MTLSAuthenticator.userIdentity` does for an mTLS login.
  - **The subject's encoding is declared, never inferred.** mTLS and PIV logins mint a username subject; a WebAuthn passkey login mints the base64url 8-byte qrdb user handle instead (`pkg/webauthn.HandleFromUserID`). The first version of this fix had `QRDBUserResolver` try `GetUserByUsername` and, on not-found, fall back to decoding the subject as a handle — review caught that this lets a **deleted** mTLS/PIV account whose username happens to also be a valid base64url encoding of a *different, live* user's numeric id resolve the refresh to that other account: identity confusion and a privilege escalation, on the exact refresh path this issue exists to close. Every identity now carries a new `sub_kind` claim/metadata key (`auth.SubjectKindMetadataKey`, values `auth.SubjectKindUsername` / `auth.SubjectKindUserHandle`), stamped by every login path that mints a pair — `MTLSAuthenticator`/PIV's `handlePIVLogin` (serves both mTLS and PIV certificate logins) sets `"username"`; `WebAuthnTokenAdapter.identityFor` sets `"user_handle"` — carried through `addIdentityClaims`/`identityFromClaims` onto both token halves. `QRDBUserResolver.lookup` now switches on the declared kind and uses **only** the matching lookup; a not-found under that kind refuses outright, with no fallback to the other encoding. A missing, empty, or unrecognized `sub_kind` refuses with `*RefreshSubjectKindError` — pre-release, so a token minted before this field existed simply fails refresh (the user logs in again); there is no compatibility shim.
  - `token.RefreshStore` gained `RevokeBySubject(ctx, subject) error`, revoking every refresh-token family belonging to a subject exactly as `RevokeFamily` revokes one; implemented in both `MemoryRefreshStore` (in-process index scan under the existing lock) and `QRDBRefreshStore` (a `Scan` over the KV refresh prefix, since the store keeps no subject index, followed by `RevokeFamily` per distinct family found). `Issuer.RevokeBySubject` is the convenience wrapper. `pkg/xkms.XKMSService.DisableUser`/`DeleteUser` — the only places in xkms that change qrdb account lifecycle (`qrdbtransport.UserClient.DisableUser`/`DeleteUser`; `EnableUser` widens access and revokes nothing) — call it for both subject encodings a login could have minted (the username, and the base64url WebAuthn handle) once the qrdb lifecycle change has already succeeded, wired via a new optional `XKMSService.SetTokenIssuer`. This is unaffected by the `sub_kind` change: `RevokeBySubject` is still keyed by the raw subject string, matched against `Record.Subject`, not by decoding it. It is defense-in-depth, not the sole enforcement: it is best-effort (a revoke failure is logged, not returned, since the lifecycle change itself must not be rolled back) and only reachable when a session-token plane is wired (`SetTokenIssuer` called); the refresh-time re-check above is what still refuses an affected session either way, including for any lifecycle change that reaches qrdb through a path other than these two xkms methods.
  - gRPC and MCP carry no refresh verb of their own (grepped for one; none found), so REST's `/api/v1/auth/refresh` was and remains the only transport this reaches.
  - Files: `pkg/auth/token/{issuer,store,errors,resolver}.go` (`resolver.go` new), `pkg/auth/{refresh_resolver.go,errors.go}` (`refresh_resolver.go` new), `pkg/api/rest/{host,handlers_auth}.go`, `pkg/server/server.go`, `pkg/xkms/{service,servicer_user}.go`.
  - Verified by: `pkg/auth/token` (`TestRefresh_UserResolver_*`, `TestRefresh_NoUserResolver_TrustsTokenClaims`, `TestMint_CarriesSubjectKindClaimAndRefreshPreservesIt`, `TestRevokeBySubject_*` run against both `RefreshStore` implementations, `TestQRDBRefreshStore_RevokeBySubject_*` error-path injection); `pkg/auth` (`TestQRDBUserResolver_*`, covering username lookup, WebAuthn-handle lookup, disabled refusal for both kinds, deleted-user refusal for both kinds, the collision regression `TestQRDBUserResolver_DeletedUsernameNeverResolvesAsAnotherUsersHandle`, a not-found/malformed handle, missing/empty/unrecognized `sub_kind`, lookup-outage fail-closed, and re-enable); `pkg/api/rest` (`TestAuthRefresh_UserResolver_*` over the actual `/api/v1/auth/refresh` HTTP path; `TestPIVLogin_Success` and `TestWebAuthnTokenAdapter_IdentityDeclaresUserHandleSubjectKind` proving each login flow stamps the correct `sub_kind`); `pkg/xkms` (`TestDisableUser_RevokesSessionsForUsernameAndWebAuthnHandle`, `TestDeleteUser_RevokesSessionsForUsernameAndWebAuthnHandle`, `TestDisableUser_RevokeFailureDoesNotFailTheOperation`, `TestDisableUser_NoTokenIssuerConfiguredStillSucceeds`). `go vet -tags "codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost" ./pkg/auth/... ./pkg/api/... ./pkg/xkms/...` and `gofmt` clean; full `go build`/`go vet` clean repo-wide.
  - Fixes #1297.
- **`types.ValidateRSAKeySize` now enforces a maximum, not just the RSAKeySize2048 minimum, closing a DoS where an authenticated caller could name an unbounded RSA modulus** (#1260). `rsa.GenerateKey` cannot be cancelled and its cost grows with the cube of the modulus size, so a request naming `key_size: 65536` pinned a CPU core for minutes to hours; nothing between the RPC surface and the crypto library refused it. The ceiling is `RSAKeySize4096`, not an arbitrary larger "safe-looking" number: it is the largest modulus every backend this project ships actually generates — AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and GCP Cloud KMS all cap asymmetric RSA CMKs at 4096 bits, a TPM 2.0 device generates at most 2048 or 3072 bits in practice, and the PKCS#11 module's own `CKM_RSA_PKCS_KEY_PAIR_GEN` already advertises 4096 as `ulMaxKeySize` after a prior 16384 advertisement let one `C_GenerateKeyPair` call exhaust the daemon's memory. `*types.RSAKeySizeError` is reused for the new refusal (message becomes "at most 4096" above the ceiling, unchanged "at least 2048" below the floor), so every call site that already type-asserts on it needs no change.
  - Two production paths generated RSA keys from a caller-controlled size without ever calling `ValidateRSAKeySize`: `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8.PKCS8Backend.generateRSAKey` duplicated only the floor check inline (no ceiling at all), and `pkg/ssh/keys.Generate`/`GenerateOnBackend` (the SSH factor's key generation, which runs entirely client-side with no backend in the loop for `Generate`) checked only `RSABits < minRSABits`. Both now call `types.ValidateRSAKeySize`. `pkg/acme/client/service`'s account/certificate-key `signerGenerators["RSA"]` had no bound at all on a config-supplied `KeyConfig.RSA.KeySize` and now validates before generating. `cmd/xkmsctl`'s local `generateKeyPair` (used by offline cert/CA issuance) and `buildKeyAttributesFromFlags` (the `xkmsctl key create`/`rotate` local pre-check ahead of the server round trip) gained the matching ceiling refusal, `ErrRSAKeySizeTooLarge`, alongside the existing `ErrRSAKeySizeTooSmall`.
  - Every other RSA-keygen path already funnelled through `types.ValidateRSAKeySize` before this change — `KeyAttributes.Validate`, the PKCS#11 and TPM backends' own `GenerateRSA`/`CreateRSA`, and `compositeBackend.GenerateRSA` (the one `Backend` implementation every `GenerateKey`/`RotateKey`/import-ceremony request reaches before any concrete backend, per its own doc comment) — so those needed no code change, only the raised ceiling from the shared validator; the PKCS#11 module's `C_GenerateKeyPair` (`pkg/pkcs11/module/mechanism.go`'s `rsaModulusBitsMax`) already enforced the identical 4096-bit ceiling for the same reason and was already consistent with the new bound.
  - Files: `pkg/types/algorithms.go`, `pkg/keyprovider/pkcs8/pkcs8.go`, `pkg/ssh/keys/generate.go`, `pkg/ssh/keys/errors.go`, `pkg/acme/client/service/account_manager.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/cert.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/key.go`, `cmd/xkmsctl/errors.go`, `sdk/go/types.go` (re-exports `RSAKeySize3072`/`RSAKeySize4096` alongside the existing `RSAKeySize2048`).
  - Verified by: `pkg/types.TestValidateRSAKeySize_RefusesAboveMaximum`/`_Table` (2047/8192/8193/16384/65536 refused, 2048/3072/4096 accepted); `pkg/xkms.TestGenerateKey_RSA_RefusesOversizedModulus` (the RPC surface refuses `key_size: 65536` in validation, before any backend runs — the test would hang rather than fail fast if that regressed); matching refusal tests in `pkg/ssh/keys`, `pkg/acme/client/service`, and `cmd/xkmsctl`. `go vet -tags "codec_cbor codec_json codec_msgpack tpm_simulator frost"` clean repo-wide, plus `-tags pkcs11` on `pkg/backend/pkcs11`; `gofmt` clean.
  - Fixes #1260.
- **A paired phone can no longer plant attestation or TLS trust anchors on the laptop through sync, and the classifier no longer grants `android-hardware` from issuer name strings** (#1304). `remote.syncTrustStore` (and the pull side of `xkey device sync`, and CA sync) imported every certificate through `truststore.AddPEM`, which auto-classifies. `ClassifyCertificate` filed any certificate whose issuer O contained "Google" and whose issuer CN contained "Attestation" as `android-hardware`, the pool `attestation.LoadTrust` verifies Android attestation against, so a phone could push a self-signed "Google ... Attestation" CA and then vouch for any device. A self-signed CA it pushed became `user-ca`, a TLS anchor for `xkey auth`.
  - New purpose `truststore.PurposeSynced` (`synced`): a quarantine no trust decision consumes. It is absent from `tlsAnchorPurposes`, and the new `truststore.IsAnchorPurpose` is false for it; the attestation verifier's pool builder now refuses any non-anchor purpose with `ErrUnsupportedPurpose`. The operator promotes a synced certificate explicitly with `xkey trust classify <fingerprint> --purpose <purpose>`.
  - `sync.TrustStoreAccessor` no longer embeds `backup.TrustStoreWriter` (the auto-classifying `AddPEM`); it requires `ImportPEM(pem, *truststore.AddCertificateOptions)`, reusing the stores' existing caller-chosen-metadata import. `ApplyTrustStoreDelta` and `ApplyCADelta` (certificate and chain) import with `Purpose: synced, Source: sync`. User-initiated imports (`xkey trust add` without `--purpose`, GUI paste/file import) keep auto-classification; trust-bootstrap imports and backup restore use explicit purposes (#1312).
  - `ClassifyCertificate` grants `android-hardware` only for a byte-exact match against the embedded Google Hardware Attestation Roots (the attestation-extension OID branch is removed in #1312). The issuer-string heuristic is gone; it also never matched Google's two RSA roots (their DN carries only a serial number), which now classify correctly.
  - The bridge `xkey device listen` and `xkey fido2` build now carries an `audit.NewSlogLogger` audit logger and the paired device's address/name as `DeviceID`/`DeviceName`. Each `remote.syncTrustStore`/`syncOATH`/`syncPasswords` write is audited as the new `audit.OpSyncApplied` (security severity), success or failure, with received/added/updated/skipped counts; a failed audit write fails the call as `ErrSyncFailed` without leaking the local error text to the phone.
  - Files: `xkey/pkg/truststore/{types,classify,import}.go`, `xkey/pkg/sync/service.go`, `xkey/pkg/attestation/verifier.go`, `xkey/pkg/audit/audit.go`, `xkey/pkg/pairing/bridge_sync.go`, `xkey/cmd/xkey/cmd/{backup,device_listen,fido2_phone_bridge,fido2_device,trust}.go`, `xkey/frontend/src/views/TrustStore.svelte`, `xkey/skills/xkey-agent/reference/cli.md`, `xkey/docs/platform-trust/`, `xkey/docs/phone-hsm/engineering.md`.
  - Verified by `TestSyncTrustStore_ForgedGoogleRootAnchorsNothing` and `TestSyncCADelta_CAAndChainAreQuarantined` (real file store, production adapter, `attestation.LoadTrust` and `TLSRoots`), `TestLoadTrust_ExcludesSyncedForgedGoogleRoot` (with a control proving the same chain verifies under `android-hardware`), `TestBridge_HandleSyncTrustStore_ForgedAnchorIsQuarantined`, `TestBridge_HandleSyncTrustStore_AuditsTheWrite`, `TestBridge_HandleSyncTrustStore_AuditFailureFailsTheCall`, `TestBridge_HandleSyncOATH_AuditsAFailedApply`, `TestBuildListenBridgeConfig_AuditsAgainstThePairedDevice`, `TestClassifyCertificate_ForgedGoogleAttestationRootIsNotAndroidHardware`, `TestClassifyCertificate_EmbeddedGoogleRootsAreAndroidHardware`. `go vet -tags "codec_json tpm_simulator ble"` clean on the affected packages; `gofmt` clean.

- **Network-fetched CA bundles and restored backups are no longer auto-classified, and the Android key attestation OID no longer grants `android-hardware`** (#1312). Three follow-ups to #1304, each a path on which someone other than the operator chose a trust anchor's purpose. The GUI's trust-strap import (`TrustService.ImportFromTrustStrap`) and `xkey trust bootstrap` imported the server's bundle through the auto-classifying `AddPEM`, while `xkey trust fetch` filed the same kind of bundle under `bootstrap-ca`. `xkey backup restore` ignored the purpose each certificate's archive entry recorded and re-classified it, which promoted a `synced` certificate out of quarantine. `ClassifyCertificate` granted `android-hardware` to any certificate carrying the Android key attestation extension (1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.1.17): a real attestation extension sits on a device leaf, never on a root, and anyone can mint a self-signed CA carrying the OID.

A missing or unrecognized recorded purpose refuses the trust-store restore before any certificate is written, with `*backup.RecordedPurposeError` (matches `ErrRestoreFailed` and `ErrMissingRecordedPurpose`/`ErrInvalidRecordedPurpose`). An operator who needs another attestation root files it with `xkey trust classify <fingerprint> --purpose android-hardware`.

- **The HashiCorp Vault backend's `tls_skip_verify` option, which disabled TLS server certificate verification, is removed — BREAKING.** `pkg/backend/vault.Backend`'s `NewBackend` (via `pkg/xkms/register_vault.go`'s `tls_skip_verify` config key) built a `vault.TLSConfig{Insecure: true}` whenever the option was set, which skips verifying the Vault server's certificate entirely and leaves the connection open to a MITM despite looking like TLS. There is no legitimate configuration this option served that a CA is not the correct fix for. `vault.Config` gains `TLSCAFile`, `TLSCAPath` (verify the server against a private or self-signed CA), and `TLSCertFile`/`TLSKeyFile` (mTLS to Vault), each wired straight into `vault.TLSConfig`'s `CACert`/`CAPath`/`ClientCert`/`ClientKey`; `Config.Validate` refuses a `TLSCertFile` set without its `TLSKeyFile` or vice versa. A deployment that set `tls_skip_verify: true` must point `tls_ca_file`/`tls_ca_path` at the Vault server's CA instead, or use `http://` for a genuinely TLS-less dev server — there is no in-band way to skip verification of an `https://` connection.
  - Extended `make check-insecure-tls` (now `scripts/check-insecure-tls.sh`, replacing the inline Makefile grep) to also catch a non-literal `InsecureSkipVerify:`/`.InsecureSkipVerify =` value (not just the literal `true`), `Insecure: true` anywhere under `pkg/backend/vault`, and `insecure.NewCredentials()` in production code without a trailing `// insecure-ok: ...` justification comment. The existing `InsecureSkipVerify` allowlist (`pkg/crypto/spki/spki.go`, `pkg/trust/fetcher/spki.go`, `pkg/trust/bootstrap/tofu_tls.go`) is unchanged. Every pre-existing production `insecure.NewCredentials()` call site now carries an inline justification: the two explicit-client-config transports (`pkg/api/transport/grpc/transport.go`, `pkg/acme/api/grpc/adapter.go`'s TCP branch), three Unix-domain-socket transports with no network path for a MITM (`pkg/api/transport/unix/transport.go`, `pkg/acme/api/grpc/adapter.go`'s Unix branch), two further explicit-client-config gRPC clients (`sdk/go/client/ssh/grpc.go`, `xkey/pkg/agent/client.go`), and GCP KMS's local-emulator-only path (`pkg/backend/gcpkms/gcpkms.go`, already gated by `Config.Validate` to a custom `Endpoint`). `_test.go` files are excluded from the `insecure.NewCredentials()` check, matching the existing gate's scope: bufconn and other in-memory test transports have no network path for a MITM and are pervasive in this tree's test suites.

A registration whose authenticator reported an already-registered credential ID therefore replaced the owner's public key and user handle. `Save` now creates only: the qrdb store uses `PutIfAbsent`, the backend store `storage.Backend.PutIfAbsent`, and all three return `ErrCredentialAlreadyExists` with the stored record untouched (REST browser finish: 409 `credential_exists`). `Update` — the path a login's sign counter, clone flag and last-used time take — now also requires the stored credential to belong to the user the update names (`ErrCredentialOwnerMismatch`); the qrdb store's `Update` is a `CompareAndSwap` against the record it checked, so a credential deleted or replaced concurrently is never resurrected (`ErrCredentialUpdateConflict`). The backend store's `Update` no longer routes through `Save` (which would now refuse it).

It now calls `Service.BeginLoginForEmail` / `BeginLoginForHandle`, which answer an unknown email or user ID, or an account without credentials, with a real go-webauthn ceremony against a decoy account whose `allowCredentials` (one or two descriptors, realistic ID lengths and transports) are derived with HKDF-SHA256 (HMAC-based, stdlib `crypto/hkdf`) from a per-process key and the requested email or handle, so repeated probes see the same descriptors. The decoy session is stored like any other; finishing against it fails as `verification_failed` (a session whose handle resolves to no account is now a verification failure, not a 500). The webauthn configuration carries no server secret, so the key is drawn with `crypto/rand` in `NewService` and held only in memory: decoys differ across restarts and cluster nodes. The SDK and gRPC `BeginAuthentication` use the same method; `FinishAuthentication` no longer re-resolves the email (the session decides the account), so an unknown email fails exactly like a wrong assertion.

Known limitation, noted in code: a provisioned account with no passkey still gets 200 until go-xkms#1294 part B is ruled.
